At a high level, how do diffusion models: Diffusion models start from pure random noise and iteratively 'denoise' it over many steps, guided by a trained model that predicts how to remove noise at each step toward an image matching the input prompt (via a text encoder conditioning the process) - the final image emerges gradually across the whole canvas simultaneously. This is conceptually very different from an LLM, which generates text autoregressively, one token at a time, each new token conditioned on everything generated so far - diffusion refines a whole output progressively, while LLMs build an output sequentially token by token.
What are common enterprise use cases for: Document summarization and information extraction from unstructured text (contracts, reports, support tickets), code generation and code review assistance, synthetic data generation for testing or augmenting scarce training data, content drafting (marketing copy, documentation, meeting notes), and data transformation/normalization tasks (converting unstructured input into structured formats) - the common thread across these is using generative AI for tasks that previously required significant manual human effort to read, write, or transform content, not just conversational interfaces.
What ethical and legal considerations (c: Copyright: understand the provenance and licensing of training data for any model used, and the legal uncertainty around whether generated output could infringe on training data sources, especially for image/video generation. Bias: generative models can reproduce and amplify biases present in training data (in generated images, text, or recommendations), requiring active testing across demographic dimensions before launch. Deepfakes/misuse: any feature capable of generating realistic synthetic media (voice, image, video) needs misuse-prevention design (watermarking, usage restrictions, identity verification for sensitive use cases) considered from the start, not bolted on after a misuse incident.
How would you detect and mitigate bias i: Detect bias by systematically testing outputs across varied inputs representing different demographics/contexts and measuring whether outcomes differ in problematic ways (e.g. generated images skewing heavily toward one demographic for a neutral prompt, or text outputs reflecting stereotypes) - this requires a deliberate, structured test set, not just spot-checking a few examples. Mitigate through a combination of prompt engineering (explicit neutrality instructions), fine-tuning or RLHF adjustments if you control the model, output filtering for clearly problematic content, and - since bias can never be fully eliminated - transparent communication to users about the system's known limitations.
What is content moderation for generativ: Content moderation screens generated output (and often input) for unsafe categories - violence, sexual content, hate speech, self-harm content, or other policy violations - before it reaches end users. Design this as a dedicated pipeline stage: a classifier (a purpose-built moderation model, or a general-purpose LLM prompted specifically for classification) scores every generated output against policy categories, with outputs above a risk threshold blocked, flagged for human review, or regenerated - this should be a mandatory pipeline stage for any user-facing generative feature, not an optional afterthought, since a single bad output can cause significant reputational or legal harm.
How would you evaluate the quality of ge: Use automated proxy metrics where they exist and correlate with actual quality (perplexity for text fluency, FID/CLIP score for image-text alignment), combined with LLM-as-judge or a trained classifier scoring against a defined rubric for dimensions automated metrics miss (creativity, appropriateness, adherence to brand voice). Sample a percentage of outputs for human review as a calibration check on whatever automated scoring you rely on, since automated metrics can drift from what actually matters to users if not periodically validated against real human judgment.
What is synthetic data generation, and w: Synthetic data generation uses a generative model to create artificial training examples, useful when real data is scarce, expensive to label, or contains sensitive information that can't be used directly (synthetic data can preserve statistical properties without exposing real individuals' data). It's a legitimate strategy for augmenting genuinely scarce data or enabling privacy-preserving training, but risky when used to paper over a fundamental lack of real, representative data - a model trained heavily on synthetic data can learn the generating model's own biases/artifacts rather than the true underlying distribution, so synthetic data should generally supplement, not fully replace, real data, and should be validated against real held-out data before trusting a model trained on it.
How would you design a system to waterma: For watermarking, embed an imperceptible but detectable signal into generated content at creation time (statistical patterns in generated text token choices, or pixel-level patterns in generated images) that a matching detector can later identify - this requires control over the generation process itself, so it only works for content you generate, not for detecting arbitrary AI content from elsewhere. For detection of content you didn't generate, use a trained classifier looking for statistical artifacts characteristic of generative models - acknowledging this is an inherently harder and less reliable problem than watermarking your own output, and detection accuracy degrades as generative models improve and produce output statistically closer to real content.
What is the difference between a foundat: A foundation model is a large, general-purpose model trained on broad data, capable of a wide range of tasks via prompting alone without further training. A fine-tuned/specialized model has been further trained on domain-specific data to excel at a narrower task, at the cost of that additional training investment and ongoing maintenance as the domain evolves. For build-vs-buy, using a foundation model via prompting is almost always the right starting point (fastest to ship, lowest investment) - only invest in fine-tuning once you've validated that prompting alone genuinely can't achieve the needed quality/consistency for your specific narrow task, since fine-tuning adds real ongoing cost and complexity that isn't justified until proven necessary.
How would you estimate and control the c: Estimate cost per request (based on expected token usage or generation complexity) multiplied by projected volume, and validate that estimate against a limited beta/canary launch before committing to full rollout, since real usage patterns (prompt length, feature adoption rate) often differ from initial assumptions. Control cost with the same levers used for any LLM cost optimization - caching repeated requests, routing simple cases to cheaper/smaller models, setting per-user or per-feature rate limits/quotas, and monitoring cost per active user continuously post-launch so a usage pattern shift or a bug causing excessive calls is caught quickly rather than discovered at the next billing cycle.
